title: OLake Iceberg REST Catalog Setup and Configuration
text:
OLake Iceberg REST Catalog Setup and Configuration | OLake Go > Destinations > Apache Iceberg > Catalogs > REST Catalog [Apache Polaris]

## Setup Steps:

1. Save the following as `docker-compose.yml`:

```docker-compose.yml
services:
  polaris:
    image: apache/polaris:1.1.0-incubating
    container_name: polaris
    ports:
      - "8181:8181"
    networks:
      - polaris-network

networks:
  polaris-network:
    driver: bridge
```

2. Start the services:

```bash
docker-compose up -d
```

3. Get Polaris root credentials from logs:

```bash
docker logs polaris | grep --text "root principal credentials"
```

Look for a line similar to:

```text
realm: default-realm root principal credentials: bd0b5cde9ffb3966:9c377f72a27ba22c47e26cd53423fa96
```

In case, you cannot find it, run **docker logs polaris** to check for the credentials.

Extract the credentials:

title: OLake Iceberg REST Catalog Setup and Configuration
text:
OLake Iceberg REST Catalog Setup and Configuration | OLake Go > Destinations > Apache Iceberg > Catalogs > REST Catalog > Setup Steps: [Apache Polaris]

- **Client ID**: `bd0b5cde9ffb3966`
- **Client Secret**: `9c377f72a27ba22c47e26cd53423fa96`

4. Get bearer token for API requests (replace `<client_id>` and `<client_secret>` with the root credential):

```bash
curl -i -X POST \
  http://localhost:8181/api/catalog/v1/oauth/tokens \
  -d 'grant_type=client_credentials&client_id=<client_id>&client_secret=<client_secret>&scope=PRINCIPAL_ROLE:ALL'
```

5. Setup an AWS S3 bucket.
6. Create an AWS IAM Role with the following policy attached:

**S3 Access Policy:**

title: OLake Iceberg REST Catalog Setup and Configuration
text:
OLake Iceberg REST Catalog Setup and Configuration | OLake Go > Destinations > Apache Iceberg > Catalogs > REST Catalog > Setup Steps: [Apache Polaris]

```json
{
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [
        {
            "Effect": "Allow",
            "Action": [
                "s3:GetObject",
                "s3:PutObject",
                "s3:DeleteObject",
                "s3:ListBucket"
            ],
            "Resource": [
                "arn:aws:s3:::your-bucket-name",
                "arn:aws:s3:::your-bucket-name/*"
            ]
        }
    ]
}
```

For detailed instructions on creating and attaching the IAM role to your EC2 instance, refer to the IAM setup guide.

The IAM role ARN will be in the format:

```text
arn:aws:iam::############:role/polaris-lakehouse-role
```

Copy this ARN as it will be needed in the next step.

> **Info:**
> When setting up **OLake**, ensure OLake runs on an instance with the same **AWS IAM Role** and **Region** configured as used for Polaris.

title: OLake Iceberg REST Catalog Setup and Configuration
text:
OLake Iceberg REST Catalog Setup and Configuration | OLake Go > Destinations > Apache Iceberg > Catalogs > REST Catalog > Setup Steps: [Apache Polaris]

7. Create catalog (replace `<bearer_token>` with token received in previous steps, `your-bucket-name` with the S3 bucket name, and `<your-iam-role-arn>` with the ARN from step 6):

```bash
curl -i -X POST http://localhost:8181/api/management/v1/catalogs \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <bearer_token>" \
  -H 'Accept: application/json' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "name": "olake_catalog",
    "type": "INTERNAL",
    "properties": {
      "default-base-location": "s3://your-bucket-name"
    },
    "storageConfigInfo": {
      "storageType": "S3",
      "roleArn": "<your-iam-role-arn>",
      "allowedLocations": ["s3://your-bucket-name"]
    }
  }'
```

8. Create user and assign roles (replace `<bearer_token>` with your bearer token). The create user command's response includes the new user's client credentials.

title: OLake Iceberg REST Catalog Setup and Configuration
text:
OLake Iceberg REST Catalog Setup and Configuration | OLake Go > Destinations > Apache Iceberg > Catalogs > REST Catalog > Setup Steps: [Apache Polaris]

```bash
# Create user (output includes client_id and client_secret, note them required in olake configuration)
curl -i -X POST "http://localhost:8181/api/management/v1/principals" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <bearer_token>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name": "olake_user", "type": "user"}'

# Create principal role
curl -i -X POST "http://localhost:8181/api/management/v1/principal-roles" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <bearer_token>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"principalRole": {"name": "olake_user_role"}}'

# Assign role to user
curl -i -X PUT "http://localhost:8181/api/management/v1/principals/olake_user/principal-roles" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <bearer_token>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"principalRole": {"name": "olake_user_role"}}'

# Create catalog role
curl -i -X POST "http://localhost:8181/api/management/v1/catalogs/olake_catalog/catalog-roles" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <bearer_token>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"catalogRole": {"name": "olake_catalog_role"}}'

# Assign catalog role to principal role
curl -i -X PUT "http://localhost:8181/api/management/v1/principal-roles/olake_user_role/catalog-roles/olake_catalog" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <bearer_token>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
```

title: OLake Iceberg REST Catalog Setup and Configuration
text:
OLake Iceberg REST Catalog Setup and Configuration | OLake Go > Destinations > Apache Iceberg > Catalogs > REST Catalog > Setup Steps: [Apache Polaris]

```bash
  -d '{"catalogRole": {"name": "olake_catalog_role"}}'

# Grant privileges
curl -i -X PUT "http://localhost:8181/api/management/v1/catalogs/olake_catalog/catalog-roles/olake_catalog_role/grants" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <bearer_token>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"grant": {"type": "catalog", "privilege": "CATALOG_MANAGE_CONTENT"}}'
```

> **Note:**
> All services involved in the sync process — including the OLake source image, Polaris, and any other dependencies — must be part of the same Docker network or accessible via network configuration.
>
> While setting up REST Catalog URI for Polaris, in any case, if either `localhost` or `host.docker.internal` do not work in place of hostname, you can pass the machine IP where Polaris is hosted.

**Important Notes:**

- The `olake_user` credentials (not root credentials) must be used for the final OLake configuration.
- The IAM role ARN is required for S3 access permissions.
- The AWS region must match across all configurations.

## Troubleshooting

- Invalid OAuth2 credentials (401 Unauthorized)

  - Cause: Incorrect or expired OAuth2 client credentials
  - Fix:

    - Verify that **client_id**, **client_secret**, **scope**, and token endpoint match your Polaris configuration.
    - Refresh tokens if expired
- Permission Denied on S3 Bucket

  - Cause: Missing or incorrect IAM permissions.
  - Fix:

    - Ensure the IAM Role ARN configured for Polaris has the following permissions on your bucket:

      - `s3:GetObject`
      - `s3:PutObject`
      - `s3:DeleteObject`
      - `s3:ListBucket`
    - Confirm the bucket name matches exactly, including letter case.
    - If using prefixes, check that your role has access to the correct path (e.g., mybucket/tenant-prefix/*)
- Connection Errors to Polaris REST API

  - Cause: The REST service is not reachable
  - Fix:

title: OLake Iceberg REST Catalog Setup and Configuration
text:
OLake Iceberg REST Catalog Setup and Configuration | OLake Go > Destinations > Apache Iceberg > Catalogs > REST Catalog > Troubleshooting [Apache Polaris]

    - Confirm that the Polaris REST service is running and accessible on the correct port (default is `8181`).
    - Ensure the service is reachable from your OLake environment; verify Docker network connectivity or firewall rules if self-hosted.
    - If TLS is enabled, check that certificates are trusted and correctly configured

**Tab: BigLake**

**BigLake** is Google Cloud's fully managed lakehouse solution that provides an Apache Iceberg REST catalog endpoint. It enables seamless interoperability across query engines like Apache Spark, BigQuery, and other compatible tools, with built-in support for Google Cloud authentication and fine-grained access control.

> **Note: BigLake Catalog Supported for v0.9.1 and above:**
> BigLake catalog support is available in OLake Go version **0.9.1** and above.

## Prerequisites

**Required services**:

- **Google Cloud Project** – with billing enabled and the BigLake API activated.
- **Cloud Storage Bucket** – for storing Iceberg table data and metadata.
- **BigLake Catalog** – created in Google Cloud.
- **Service Account** – with appropriate BigLake and Cloud Storage permissions.

**Required permissions**:

- **Service Account Roles**:

  - `BigLake Editor` (`roles/biglake.editor`) – for writing table data.
  - `Storage Object User` (`roles/storage.objectUser`) – on all associated Cloud Storage buckets.

For detailed setup instructions, prerequisites, and IAM configuration, refer to the Google Cloud BigLake REST Catalog documentation.

## Prerequisites

- **Database**: A Snowflake database where OLake Go will create Iceberg tables. The database must have its catalog and external volume configured as SNOWFLAKE and SNOWFLAKE_MANAGED respectively:

  ```sql
  ALTER DATABASE <your_database_name> SET CATALOG = 'SNOWFLAKE';
  ALTER DATABASE <your_database_name> SET EXTERNAL_VOLUME = 'SNOWFLAKE_MANAGED';
  ```

  > **Note:**
  > If you use external storage (AWS, GCP, Azure) instead of Snowflake-managed storage, set `EXTERNAL_VOLUME` to the name of your external volume being used.
- **Role**: A Snowflake role with database usage privileges and permission to create schemas, assigned to the user OLake Go will use for authentication. If the database uses an external volume other than `SNOWFLAKE_MANAGED`, this role must also have access to that external volume.
- **Authentication Policy**: An authentication policy that allows your chosen authentication method, attached to the user.
- **Account identifier**: Your Snowflake account identifier uses the form `<org>-<account>`. Look it up with:

  ```sql

  ```

## Troubleshooting

### Common Issues

1. **Database or role name mismatch (case sensitivity)**: Snowflake uppercases unquoted identifiers. If `CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS snow` is run, or a role is created without double quotes, Snowflake stores the name as `SNOW`, not `snow`. If double quotes are used (`CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS "snow"`), the name is stored exactly as written. OLake Go must use the same spelling and casing as created in Snowflake.

# Google Cloud Storage (GCS) Writer Overview

Currently OLake Go supports writing data to Google Cloud Storage (GCS), using `Hive Catalog` that supports Iceberg. This allows you to leverage GCS as a scalable and durable storage solution for your data lakehouse architecture.

title: OLake Iceberg Partitioning for Faster Queries
text:
OLake Iceberg Partitioning for Faster Queries | OLake Go > Destinations > Apache Iceberg

# Iceberg Partitioning Support

Partitioning groups rows that share common values at **write-time**, so that queries filtering on those values read only the relevant files. The result is **fewer data files scanned, less I/O, and faster queries**.

OLake Go allows seamless writing into **partitioned Iceberg tables**, supporting all built-in transformations in **Apache Iceberg™**.

## How Iceberg Handles Partitions?

Apache Iceberg stores partition data in both its metadata and manifest files to enable **efficient querying** and **file pruning**. Rather than embedding partition information in file paths, Iceberg records the partition values for each file in manifests and maintains a snapshot-based metadata tree that tracks those manifests.

When you run a query like `WHERE date > …`, Iceberg consults the metadata to skip over any data files whose recorded partition values cannot satisfy the filter.

### Key Features

- Hidden partitioning
- Evolvable specs
- Rich partition transforms
- Manifest metadata
- Snapshot isolation
- Efficient pruning

Learn more about Iceberg Partitioning.

## How to Add a Partition in OLake Go?

When adding a partition, you need to configure two components:

| Component | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **field_name** | Column in the table (**created_at**, **user_id**, etc.) |
| **transform** | Iceberg transform that converts the value, e.g., **identity** |

**Example 1: Time-based partitioning for event data**

```text
/{event_date, day}/{event_hour, hour}
```

- Partitions data by day and hour for efficient time-range queries
- Useful for analytics workloads with time-based filtering

**Example 2: Geographic and temporal partitioning**

```text
/{region, identity}/{created_at, month}
```

- Partitions by geographic region and creation month
- Ideal for multi-region applications with time-based analysis

Check all the available transforms below.

> **Warning: Resource Requirements for High Partition Counts:**
> When configuring partitions, consider the RAM requirements based on your partition count and thread configuration:
>
> **RAM Calculation (Historical Load & Parallel-table based CDC - MongoDB/Kafka sources):**
>
> - Each partition writer can consume approximately **20-50 MB** of RAM when processing data
> - Total RAM needed ≈ **Number of threads × Number of partitions × 20-50 MB**
> - Example: With 10 threads and 1000 partitions, you may need **256-512 GB RAM**
>
> **Instance Sizing Recommendations:**
>
> - For high partition counts (1000+ partitions with multiple threads), use a **512 GB RAM instance**
> - For very high partition counts, consider scaling to a **1 TB RAM instance**
>
> **Mitigation Strategies:**
>
> - **Reduce thread count**: Lowering the number of threads reduces concurrent partition writers and RAM usage
> - **Optimize partition granularity**: Avoid creating too many small partitions; aim for partitions with meaningful data volumes

For hierarchical partitioning, you can have multiple `/{field_name, transform}` entries in the **Partition regex**. Example: `/{created_at, year}/{user_id, bucket[32]}`

> **Info: Special case:**
> You may use `now()` as a pseudo-column that evaluates to the **_olake_timestamp** column which is the writer's current timestamp (useful when your records lack a suitable time field).

## Supported Transformations

All transforms create partition folders with predictable naming patterns for efficient querying:

title: OLake Iceberg Partitioning for Faster Queries
text:
OLake Iceberg Partitioning for Faster Queries | OLake Go > Destinations > Apache Iceberg > Iceberg Partitioning Support > Supported Transformations

| Transform | Typical use-case | How It Works | Spec Snippet | Example Input → Partition Value |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **`identity`** | Columns with only a few distinct values – e.g. country, status | Writes the raw value unchanged | `/{status, identity}` | `status = 'active'` → folder `status=active/` |
| **`year`** | Time-series data where queries slice whole years | Extracts the calendar year as an integer | `/{created_at, year}` | `created_at = 2025-04-24 15:42` → `year=2025/` |
| **`month`** | Monthly reporting, rollups, retention | Returns the month number (1-12) of the timestamp | `/{created_at, month}` | `created_at = 2025-04-24 15:42` → `month=4/` |
| **`day`** | Daily dashboards, 30-day TTL jobs | Returns the local calendar day (1-31) | `/{event_date, day}` | `event_date = 2025-04-24` → `day=24/` |
| **`hour`** | High-volume logs where analysts drill into single hours | Returns hour-of-day (0-23) | `/{event_time, hour}` | `event_time = 2025-04-24 15:42` → `hour=15/` |
| **`bucket[N]`** | Very high-cardinality keys (email, UUID) to distribute writes | Hashes the value and assigns it to **N** numbered buckets (0…N-1) | `/{user_id, bucket[64]}` | `user_id = 'f47ac10b...'` → `user_id_bucket=17/` _(one of 64)_ |

title: OLake Iceberg Partitioning for Faster Queries
text:
OLake Iceberg Partitioning for Faster Queries | OLake Go > Destinations > Apache Iceberg > Iceberg Partitioning Support > Supported Transformations

| Transform | Typical use-case | How It Works | Spec Snippet | Example Input → Partition Value |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **`truncate[N]`** | Long strings where only the prefix matters (domains, URLs) | Keeps the first **N** UTF-8 characters | `/{domain, truncate[4]}` | `domain = 'example.com'` → `domain=exam/` |
| **`void`** | Dropping partition fields without removing from spec | Always produces null values | `/{old_field, void}` | `old_field = 'any_value'` → `old_field=null/` |

> **Info: Void Transform and Non-Linear Transformations:**
> The **void transform** in Apache Iceberg always produces null values regardless of input. It effectively **drops** a partition field without removing it from the partition specification. Starting from Iceberg V2, it is used when dropping a partition field.
>
> **Non-linear transformations** like `bucket` and `void` do not preserve ordering, meaning there's no predictable relationship between input values and their transformed output positions.

title: OLake Iceberg Partitioning for Faster Queries
text:
OLake Iceberg Partitioning for Faster Queries | OLake Go > Destinations > Apache Iceberg > Iceberg Partitioning Support

> **Warning: Important:**
> Iceberg does not support redundant fields during partitioning, even with different transforms on the same column. Avoid applying multiple time transforms to the same column in a single partition specification.
>
> **Redundant transform combinations:**
>
> - `year(ts)` is redundant with `month(ts)`, `hour(ts)`, `day(ts)`
> - `month(ts)` is redundant with `hour(ts)` and `day(ts)`
> - `day(ts)` is redundant with `hour(ts)` For example, this is incorrect: **`/{timestamp_col, hour}/{timestamp_col, minute}`**

## Putting it all together

Let's look at a real-world example of an e-commerce analytics table with three partitions for optimal query performance.

### Example: E-commerce Events Table

**Partition Configuration:**

```text
/{event_date, day}/{region, identity}/{user_id, bucket[256]}
```

This creates a hierarchical partitioning strategy:

1. **Daily partitions** for time-based queries
2. **Regional partitions** for geographic analysis
3. **User bucketing** to distribute high-cardinality data

├── metadata/
│   ├── v0.metadata.json
│   ├── v1.metadata.json
│   ├── snap-0001.avro
│   └── manifest-01.avro
└── data/
    ├── event_date_day=2025-01-15/
    │   ├── region=us-east/
    │   │   └── user_id_bucket=0/
    │   │       └── data-001.parquet
    │   └── region=eu-west/
    │       └── user_id_bucket=128/
    │           └── data-002.parquet

title: OLake Iceberg Partitioning for Faster Queries
text:
OLake Iceberg Partitioning for Faster Queries | OLake Go > Destinations > Apache Iceberg > Iceberg Partitioning Support > Putting it all together

### SQL Query Examples

**1. Daily Report (scans only 1 day's data):**

```sql
SELECT event_type, COUNT(*)
FROM ecommerce_events
WHERE event_date = '2025-01-15'
GROUP BY event_type;
```

_Iceberg scans only: **event_date_day=2025-01-15/** directory_

**2. Regional Analysis (scans specific region across time):**

```sql
SELECT DATE(event_date) as day, SUM(revenue)
FROM ecommerce_events
WHERE region = 'us-east'
  AND event_date BETWEEN '2025-01-15' AND '2025-01-17'
GROUP BY DATE(event_date);
```

_Iceberg scans only: **region=us-east/** subdirectories within the date range_

#### Performance Benefits

- **Time queries**: Skip irrelevant days entirely
- **Regional queries**: Skip other geographic regions
- **User queries**: Skip 255 out of 256 user buckets
- **Combined filters**: Maximum pruning when filtering on multiple partition fields

This partitioning strategy enables sub-second queries on petabyte-scale datasets by reading only the relevant data files.

text:
OLake Iceberg Partitioning for Faster Queries | OLake Go > Destinations > Apache Iceberg > Iceberg Partitioning Support

## Checklist before you decide

| Question | If Yes, Consider |
|---|---|
| **Do your workloads frequently filter by date or time?** | Use `day()`, `month()`, or `year()` transforms for time-based partitioning |
| **Do you have columns with many distinct values (user IDs, session IDs)?** | Use `bucket(n)` to evenly distribute high-cardinality data into n buckets |
| **Do you have columns with few distinct values (country, status)?** | Direct partitioning on the column using `identity` transform is sufficient |
| **Do your queries often target numeric ranges (price, timestamps)?** | Use `truncate(width)` to group values into fixed-size ranges |
| **Do you frequently filter by region, department, or category?** | Partition by `identity` on that column for geographic/categorical grouping |
| **Might your schema or query patterns change over time?** | Choose hidden partitioning and allow spec evolution for flexibility |
| **Are you concerned about metadata overhead from too many partitions?** | Balance granularity: avoid partitions smaller than a few MB to optimize performance vs. file count |
| **Do you have data skew or potential hot partitions?** | Combine high-cardinality and low-cardinality transforms (e.g., `bucket` within `day`) |
| **Do you prioritize flat directory structures?** | Limit nested transforms to two or three levels for storage layout simplicity |

title: OLake Iceberg Partitioning for Faster Queries
text:
OLake Iceberg Partitioning for Faster Queries | OLake Go > Destinations > Apache Iceberg > Iceberg Partitioning Support > Checklist before you decide

> **Tip: Quick Reference:**
> - **Cardinality** — Aim for 100 – 10,000 files per partition folder.
> - **Skew** — Use `bucket[N]` when one value dominates (e.g., a single large tenant).
> - **Time range queries** — Put the time transform first if nearly every query filters on a date.
> - **Evolution** — Start simple (e.g., `{event_date, day}`) and add more fields later; Iceberg keeps old snapshots readable.

How to Attach IAM Role to EC2 Instance | OLake Go

# How to Attach IAM Role to EC2 Instance

This guide provides detailed instructions for configuring IAM roles and attaching them to EC2 instances to use catalogs (e.g., Apache Polaris) with AWS S3 storage.

The process involves:

1. **Trust Policy** - Allows the IAM role to assume itself (required for vended credentials)
2. **IAM Policy** - Grants necessary S3 permissions
3. **IAM Role** - Combines the trust policy and permissions
4. **Instance Profile** - Allows EC2 instances to use the role
5. **Attach to EC2** - Associate the role with your running EC2 instance

## Prerequisites

- AWS CLI installed and configured with appropriate permissions
- An existing EC2 instance
- An S3 bucket for storing Iceberg data
- IAM permissions to create roles, policies, and instance profiles

title: How to Attach IAM Role to EC2 Instance
section_path: How to Attach IAM Role to EC2 Instance

title: How to Attach IAM Role to EC2 Instance
section_path: How to Attach IAM Role to EC2 Instance
text:
How to Attach IAM Role to EC2 Instance | OLake Go

## IAM Policy for S3 Access

An IAM policy that grants access to the S3 bucket must be created. A file named `iam-policy.json` must be created:

```json title="iam-policy.json"
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "s3:GetObject",
        "s3:PutObject",
        "s3:DeleteObject",
        "s3:ListBucket"
      ],
      "Resource": [
        "arn:aws:s3:::<YOUR_S3_BUCKET>",
        "arn:aws:s3:::<YOUR_S3_BUCKET>/*"
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

> **Tip:**
> `<YOUR_S3_BUCKET>` must be replaced with the actual S3 bucket name, `<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>` with the AWS account ID, and `<YOUR_ROLE_NAME>` with the role name.

## Step-by-Step Setup

The following steps must be followed to create the IAM role and policies:

### 1. Create the IAM Policy

```bash
aws iam create-policy \
  --policy-name polaris-s3-access-policy \
  --policy-document file://iam-policy.json
```

title: How to Attach IAM Role to EC2 Instance
section_path: How to Attach IAM Role to EC2 Instance
text:
How to Attach IAM Role to EC2 Instance | OLake Go > Step-by-Step Setup

### 2. Create the IAM Role

```bash
aws iam create-role \
  --role-name polaris-lakehouse-role \
  --assume-role-policy-document file://trust-policy.json
```

### 3. Attach Policy to Role

```bash
aws iam attach-role-policy \
  --role-name polaris-lakehouse-role \
  --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>:policy/polaris-s3-access-policy
```

### 4. Create Instance Profile

```bash
aws iam create-instance-profile \
  --instance-profile-name polaris-lakehouse-profile
```

### 5. Add Role to Instance Profile

```bash
aws iam add-role-to-instance-profile \
  --instance-profile-name polaris-lakehouse-profile \
  --role-name polaris-lakehouse-role
```

### 6. Attach IAM Role to EC2 Instance

This is the crucial step that allows the EC2 instance to use the IAM role for AWS S3 access.

```bash
aws ec2 associate-iam-instance-profile \
  --instance-id <YOUR_EC2_INSTANCE_ID> \
  --iam-instance-profile Name=polaris-lakehouse-profile
```

title: How to Attach IAM Role to EC2 Instance
section_path: How to Attach IAM Role to EC2 Instance
text:
How to Attach IAM Role to EC2 Instance | OLake Go

### 7. Get the Role ARN

```bash
aws iam get-role \
  --role-name polaris-lakehouse-role \
  --query 'Role.Arn' \
  --output text
```

This will output something like:

```text
arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/polaris-lakehouse-role
```

## Verification

To verify the setup is correct:

1. **Test IAM Role from EC2 Instance** (SSH into the EC2 instance and run):

   ```bash
   # Check if instance can assume the role
   aws sts get-caller-identity

   # Test S3 access
   aws s3 ls s3://<YOUR_S3_BUCKET>
   ```

## Next Steps

After completing the IAM setup:

1. Return to the REST Catalog setup guide to continue with catalog creation
2. The Role ARN from step 7 must be used when creating the Polaris catalog
3. The setup should be tested by creating tables and querying data

## Troubleshooting

### 1. maven related issues

```text
Iceberg JAR file not found. Building with Maven...
usage: mvn [-h] [_ ...]
mvn: error: unrecognized arguments: -Dmaven.test.skip=true
```

#### Solution:

Install the correct version of Maven. Run `which mvn` or `mvn --version` to verify the Maven installation.

### 2. AWS region issues

```text
Region must be specified either via environment variable (AWS_REGION) or  system property (aws.region)., software.amazon.awssdk.regions.providers.AwsProfileRegionProvider@7a7eb56e: No region provided in profile: default, software.amazon.awssdk.regions.providers.InstanceProfileRegionProvider@241d5e60: Unable to contact EC2 metadata service.
```

#### Solution

Set the AWS region explicitly if the error occurs. For example:

```bash
export AWS_REGION=us-east-1
```

Replace us-east-1 with the appropriate region.

text:
OLake Iceberg Troubleshooting & Local Testing Guide | OLake Go > Destinations > Apache Iceberg > Troubleshooting [Troubleshooting]

### 3. Linkage error

```text
025-04-02T13:51:25Z ERROR [Java-Iceberg:50051] Error: LinkageError occurred while loading main class io.debezium.server.iceberg.OlakeRpcServer
2025-04-02T13:51:25Z ERROR [Java-Iceberg:50051] 	java.lang.UnsupportedClassVersionError: io/debezium/server/iceberg/OlakeRpcServer has been compiled by a more recent version of the Java Runtime (class file version 61.0), this version of the Java Runtime only recognizes class file versions up to 55.0
```

#### Solution

Ensure that Java version is 17 or higher. Check the installed version with:

```java
java -version
```

If the version is older, update Java to a supported version. Reload the shell configuration (e.g., source ~/.zshrc) after updating.

### 4. gRPC Connection Fail

**Cause**: The gRPC server is not running or the port configuration is incorrect.

#### Solution

- Verify that the Java gRPC server is running.
- Confirm that the port specified in destination.json matches the server port.

# S3 Parquet

OLake Go supports writing in parquet format directly to S3. Before proceeding with the S3 Parquet destination, we recommend reviewing the Getting Started and Installation sections.

## Prerequisites

- Before setting up the destination, make sure you have successfully set up the `source`.
- **AWS S3:** Review the minimum required IAM Permissions for S3 Parquet Writer.
- **GCS:** Review GCP IAM Permission for role-based access, and create HMAC keys for your service account to use as S3 credentials. See Creation of HMAC Keys below.

| **s3_endpoint** | _(Optional)_ The **custom endpoint** for S3-compatible services. **Required** for **GCS** using HMAC keys. | string | `"https://storage.googleapis.com"` |
| **s3_path** | _(Optional)_ The specific path (or prefix) within the S3 bucket where data files will be written. This is typically a folder path that starts with a `/` (e.g. `"/data"`). | string | A valid path string |

# Google Cloud Storage (GCS) Writer Overview

OLake supports writing data to Google Cloud Storage (GCS) in parquet format.

Google Cloud Storage provides an S3-compatible interface, allowing you to use S3-compatible tools and libraries to interact with GCS buckets and objects. This interoperability enables seamless integration and ingestion of data into GCS by supporting the Amazon S3 API, which means you can use existing S3 tools and workflows with minimal changes—such as updating the endpoint to `https://storage.googleapis.com` and authenticating via HMAC keys. This compatibility simplifies migrations, data transfers, and tool usage across platforms.

Add these HMAC keys as Access Key and Secret Key in the destination configuration - Parquet Writer Configuration

> **Info:**
> HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code) keys in Google Cloud Storage are used for authentication when accessing GCS resources, particularly through the S3-compatible API. They consist of an access key and a secret key, which provide a way to sign requests and verify identity without using Google account credentials. \
>
> Refer - https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/authentication/hmackeys

More details on how to configure and use the GCS writer will be available soon. In the meantime, you can refer to the Iceberg writer documentation for general guidance on Iceberg integration, as the principles are similar across different storage backends.

# Data Partitioning

OLake Go supports data partitioning when writing to S3. You can define a `partition_regex` during `schema changes` in OLake UI or in `streams.json` in OLake CLI. This regex determines how data is partitioned into folders within your S3 bucket. Partitioning is defined on a per-stream (table or collection) basis.

title: Parquet Data Partitioning for S3 in OLake
text:
Parquet Data Partitioning for S3 in OLake | OLake Go > Destinations > Parquet Writer > Data Partitioning

> **Warning: Resource Requirements for High Partition Counts:**
> When configuring partitions, consider the RAM requirements based on your partition count and thread configuration:
>
> **RAM Calculation (Historical Load & Parallel-table based CDC - MongoDB/Kafka sources):**
>
> - Each partition writer can consume approximately **20-50 MB** of RAM when processing data
> - Total RAM needed ≈ **Number of threads × Number of partitions × 20-50 MB**
> - Example: With 10 threads and 1000 partitions, you may need **256-512 GB RAM**
>
> **Instance Sizing Recommendations:**
>
> - For high partition counts (1000+ partitions with multiple threads), use a **512 GB RAM instance**
> - For very high partition counts, consider scaling to a **1 TB RAM instance**
>
> **Mitigation Strategies:**
>
> - **Reduce thread count**: Lowering the number of threads reduces concurrent partition writers and RAM usage
> - **Optimize partition granularity**: Avoid creating too many small partitions; aim for partitions with meaningful data volumes

## Partition Regex Attributes

You can partition data based on column values using the `partition_regex`. A typical partition pattern looks like:

```json
"partition_regex": "/{column_name, default_value, granularity}"
```

- **column_name:**
  _(Required)_ The name of the column whose value will determine the partition folder. You can also use the `now()` function to represent the current date.
- **default_value:**
  _(Optional)_ If the column value is null or unparseable, a default value (prefixed with `default_`) will be used. Default value is a fallback value.
- **granularity:**
  _(Optional)_ For time-based columns, you can specify the granularity. Supported values include `HH` (hour), `DD` (day), `WW` (week), `MM` (month), and `YYYY` (year). `granularity` is not needed if the `column_name` is not a timestamp field and can be left empty.

title: Parquet Data Partitioning for S3 in OLake
text:
Parquet Data Partitioning for S3 in OLake | OLake Go > Destinations > Parquet Writer > Data Partitioning

> **Info:**
> 1. Each segment enclosed between slashes (`/.../`) in the partition regex can include up to three parameters.
> 2. You can define as many directory path partitions as you wish to.
> 3. Path name other than english are also supported (as long as they are `STRING` values).

## Supported Regex Patterns

The partition regex supports several patterns to handle both column values and timestamps. Below is a summary of the supported patterns:

title: Parquet Data Partitioning for S3 in OLake
text:
Parquet Data Partitioning for S3 in OLake | OLake Go > Destinations > Parquet Writer > Data Partitioning > Supported Regex Patterns

| **Pattern** | **Description** | **Example** |
|---|---|---|
| `now()` | Uses the current local timestamp to extract date components such as day (DD), month (MM), or year (YYYY). | – |
| `default` | If a specified column does not exist, the value is treated as a constant string prefixed with `default_`. | – |
| `{col_name}` | Inserts the value of the specified column. | – |
| `{now(),2025,YYYY}` | Extracts only the year part of the current timestamp. | `2025` |
| `{now(),2025,MM}` | Extracts only the month part of the current timestamp. | `1`, `12` |
| `{now(),2025,DD}` | Extracts only the day part of the current timestamp. | `1`, `31` |
| `{now(),2025,YYYY}-{now(),06,MM}` | Combines year and month from the current timestamp. | `2025-02` |
| `{now(),2025,YYYY}-{now(),06,MM}-{now(),13,DD}` | Combines year, month, and day from the current timestamp. | `2025-02-13`, `2025-12-31` |

title: Parquet Data Partitioning for S3 in OLake
text:
Parquet Data Partitioning for S3 in OLake | OLake Go > Destinations > Parquet Writer > Data Partitioning > Supported Regex Patterns

**Usage Examples:**

- **Correct:** ✅

  - `"partition_regex": "/{title,,}/{now(),2025,DD}/{latest_version,,}"`
  - `"partition_regex": "{title,,}/{now(),2025,DD}/{latest_version,,}"`
- **Incorrect:** ❌

  - `"partition_regex": "{title},,}/{now(),2025,DD}/{latest_version,,}"`
    _(Note the misplaced comma and bracket.)_
- **Special Characters in Column Values:** When data is converted to Parquet format, escape characters or special symbols (e.g., `\u0026` for `&`) are converted to their corresponding characters while constructing the folder name. However, if a column value contains the `/` character, it will be interpreted as a directory separator, thus creating additional nested folders.

  For example, consider a column named `title` with the value:

  ```text
  Hi/my name is / priyansh
  ```

  This value will generate a nested directory structure as shown below:

title: Parquet Data Partitioning for S3 in OLake
text:
Parquet Data Partitioning for S3 in OLake | OLake Go > Destinations > Parquet Writer > Data Partitioning > Supported Regex Patterns

  ```text
  olake-s3-test
  └── data-s3
      └── test_db
          └── table1
              └── Hi
                  └── my name is 
                      └── priyansh
                          └── 423878fsd87fsd78XXXXXX.parquet
  ```

  > **Note:**
  > If you intend the entire value to be treated as a single folder name, ensure that the data does not include the `/` character or consider sanitizing your column values before ingestion.

text:
Parquet Data Partitioning for S3 in OLake | OLake Go > Destinations > Parquet Writer > Data Partitioning

## Supported Timestamp Formats for Partitioning

OLake Go attempts to parse a wide range of timestamp formats when generating partition folders. The following formats are currently supported:

```text
"2006-01-02",
"2006-01-02 15:04:05",
"2006-01-02 15:04:05 -07:00",
"2006-01-02 15:04:05-07:00",
"2006-01-02T15:04:05",
"2006-01-02T15:04:05.000000",
"2006-01-02T15:04:05.999999999Z07:00",
"2006-01-02T15:04:05+0000",
"2020-08-17T05:50:22.895Z",
"2006-01-02 15:04:05.999999-07",
"2006-01-02 15:04:05.999999+00"
```

For the latest updates or to add support for additional timestamp formats, please refer to the corresponding implementation or create an issue.

title: Parquet Data Partitioning for S3 in OLake
text:
Parquet Data Partitioning for S3 in OLake | OLake Go > Destinations > Parquet Writer > Data Partitioning > Supported Timestamp Formats for Partitioning

For a column mname that is a timestamp, replace `now()` with the name of the column and specify which value you want to extract from the timestamp field.

```json
"partition_regex": "{timestamp_column,2025,YYYY}-{timestamp_column,12,MM}-{timestamp_column,13,DD}"
```

title: Parquet Data Partitioning for S3 in OLake
text:
Parquet Data Partitioning for S3 in OLake | OLake Go > Destinations > Parquet Writer > Data Partitioning

## Key-Value Format Partitioning

In addition to our dynamic timestamp-based partitioning, we also support key-value style partitioning—a format commonly used in the data engineering industry. This allows you to create directory structures that directly reflect attribute values from your data records. For example, you can have partitions that look like:

```text
age=26/city=delhi/type=new
```

This is achieved by combining static text (like `age=`, `city=`, and `type=`) with dynamic column value extraction via the `partition_regex`. The general pattern we support is:

```json
"partition_regex": "/{column_name, default_value, granularity}"
```

To create key-value formatted partitions, you simply embed your column placeholders within the desired key format. For instance, you can configure your partitioning as follows:

```json
"partition_regex": "/age={age_column, default_age,}/city={city_column, default_city,}/type={type_column, default_type,}"
```

In this example:

title: Parquet Data Partitioning for S3 in OLake
text:
Parquet Data Partitioning for S3 in OLake | OLake Go > Destinations > Parquet Writer > Data Partitioning > Key-Value Format Partitioning

- `age={age_column, default_age,}` extracts the value from the column representing age. If the value is missing, it falls back to `default_age`.
- `city={city_column, default_city,}` does the same for city.
- `type={type_column, default_type,}` does the same for type.

title: Parquet Data Partitioning for S3 in OLake
text:
Parquet Data Partitioning for S3 in OLake | OLake Go > Destinations > Parquet Writer > Data Partitioning > Key-Value Format Partitioning

### Examples

1. **Partitioning with Mixed Static and Dynamic Text**

   You can also mix static text with dynamic values to create clearer partition names. For example:

   ```json
   "partition_regex": "/age={age,unknown,}/location=city-{city,unknown,}/type={type,default,}"
   ```

   For a record like:

   ```json
   {
     "age": "30",
     "city": "mumbai",
     "type": "existing"
   }
   ```

   the path will be:

   ```text
   s3://your_bucket/age=30/location=city-mumbai/type=existing/<filename>.parquet
   ```

2. **Composite Partitions Including Date**

   It’s also possible to combine key-value pairs with date-based partitioning. For instance:

   ```json
   "partition_regex": "/dt={now(),2025,YYYY}-{now(),06,MM}-{now(),13,DD}/country={country,default_country,}/city={city,default_city,}"
   ```

   This would produce paths like:

title: Parquet Data Partitioning for S3 in OLake
text:
Parquet Data Partitioning for S3 in OLake | OLake Go > Destinations > Parquet Writer > Data Partitioning > Key-Value Format Partitioning

   ```text
   s3://your_bucket/dt=2025-02-18/country=USA/city=NewYork/<filename>.parquet
   ```

### Common Patterns in the Industry

- **Date-Based Partitions:**

  - Format: `/dt={now(),2025,YYYY}-{now(),06,MM}-{now(),13,DD}`
  - Use case: Simplifies range queries by maintaining ISO8601 date order.
- **Categorical Partitions:**

  - Format: `/country={country,default_country,}/state={state,default_state,}`
  - Use case: Effective for geo-segmentation and filtering data by regions.
- **Composite Attribute Partitions:**

  - Format: `/age={age,default_age,}/city={city,default_city,}/type={type,default_type,}`
  - Use case: Offers detailed segmentation based on multiple attributes, which can enhance query performance and improve data organization.

> **Note:**
> In the above examples, the third key is empty denoting its optional for column types that are non `TIMESTAMP` based.

title: IAM Permissions - Parquet Writer
text:
IAM Permissions - Parquet Writer | OLake Go > Destinations > Parquet Writer

# IAM Permissions Required

## 1. AWS (Amazon Web Services) IAM Policy

To successfully sync your source data with S3, ensure that your AWS IAM policy grants at least minimal permissions for listing, creating, reading, and writing to the S3 bucket. Below is a sample IAM policy.

```json
{
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [
        {
            "Sid": "S3BucketReadWrite",
            "Effect": "Allow",
            "Action": [
                "s3:ListBucket",
                "s3:GetBucket*",
                "s3:*Object"
            ],
            "Resource": [
                "arn:aws:s3:::{S3_BUCKET_NAME}",
                "arn:aws:s3:::{S3_BUCKET_NAME}/*"
            ]
        },
        {
            "Sid": "ListAllBuckets",
            "Effect": "Allow",
            "Action": "s3:ListAllMyBuckets",
            "Resource": "*"
        }
    ]
}
```

## 2. GCS (Google Cloud Storage) IAM Policy

To successfully sync source data using GCS, ensure that GCS IAM policy grants at least minimal permission for listing, creating, reading, and writing to S3 bucket.

title: IAM Permissions - Parquet Writer
text:
IAM Permissions - Parquet Writer | OLake Go > Destinations > Parquet Writer > IAM Permissions Required > 2. GCS (Google Cloud Storage) IAM Policy

### Using GCloud CLI

- Create a service account in GCS. Install Google Cloud SDK (gcloud CLI). Initialize the SDK using `gcloud init` command.
- Login to GCS account, use `gcloud auth login` command.
- Set the preferred project ID, use `gcloud config set project Project-ID`. Replace 'Project-ID' with your actual project id.
- Create minimal set of IAM role required for the sync to GCS bucket.

  ```bash
  gcloud iam roles create storage.customAccess \
  --project="$(gcloud config get-value project)" \
  --file=/user-preferred-directory/gcs_policy.yaml
  ```

- Sample gcs_policy.yaml with minimal set of permissions required.

  ```yaml title="gcs_policy.yaml"
  title: Custom Storage Access
  description: Equivalent to AWS S3 policy (List/Get bucket, full object access, list all buckets)
  stage: GA
  includedPermissions:
  - storage.buckets.getIamPolicy
  - storage.buckets.get
  - storage.buckets.list
  - storage.objects.list
  - storage.objects.get
  - storage.objects.create
  - storage.objects.delete
  - storage.objects.update
  ```

title: IAM Permissions - Parquet Writer
text:
IAM Permissions - Parquet Writer | OLake Go > Destinations > Parquet Writer > IAM Permissions Required > 2. GCS (Google Cloud Storage) IAM Policy

- Replace 'Project-ID' and 'gcs-based-service-account' with actual GCS project id and service account.

  ```json title="gcs_rolebinding.json"
  {
  "bindings": [
          {
              "role": "projects/Project-ID/roles/storage.customAccess",
              "members": [
              "serviceAccount:gcs-based-service-account.com"
              ]
          }
      ]
  }
  ```

- Bind the role to service account.

  ```bash
  gcloud storage buckets set-iam-policy \
  gs://<bucket-name> \
  /user-preferred-directory/gcs_rolebinding.json
  ```

- Create a GCS bucket and HMAC keys for the service account for whom the above role is defined.

### Using GCP

- Create a project.
- Creating service account - permissions can be given then and there as well.
- Create a GCS bucket and HMAC keys for the service account

title: Troubleshooting - Parquet Writer
text:
Troubleshooting - Parquet Writer | OLake Go > Destinations > Parquet Writer

# Troubleshooting S3 Writer

## 1. Failed to create AWS session

```bash
Symptom: failed to create AWS session: invalid configuration
```

**Cause:**

- Missing or invalid AWS credentials (`AccessKey`, `SecretKey`).
- Misconfigured region or endpoint for S3.

**Resolution:**

- Ensure `Bucket`, `Region`, and authentication values are correctly set in configuration.
- If using AWS IAM roles (EC2/ECS/EKS), you **do not need explicit keys**, but make sure the role is attached with correct permissions.
- For **MinIO / GCS S3-compatible endpoints**, ensure that all **valid keys** are provided.

title: Troubleshooting - Parquet Writer
text:
Troubleshooting - Parquet Writer | OLake Go > Destinations > Parquet Writer > Troubleshooting S3 Writer

## 2. S3 Credentials or Permissions Errors

```bash
Symptom: failed to write test file to S3: AccessDenied: Access Denied OR failed to upload file to S3 ... 403 Forbidden
```

**Cause:**

- The AWS credentials supplied to OLake Go do **not** have the minimum set of S3 actions or the bucket ARN is incorrect.

**Resolution:**

- Make sure the IAM user / role has the JSON policy shown in the IAM Permissions page attached.
- If you use temporary credentials (STS), check that the session is still valid.
- Verify that the bucket name in the policy and in the destination configuration are identical (case-sensitive).
- For **MinIO** or **GCS**, ensure `S3Endpoint` is set in the destination config.

title: OLake Go product FAQ
text:
OLake Go product FAQ | olake.io product page

### How to get started?

Check the Quickstart Guide. With a single Docker command you can spin up OLake Go and access the UI.

title: OLake Go product FAQ
section_path: Is OLake Go really open source?
text:
OLake Go product FAQ | olake.io product page

### Is OLake Go really open source?

Yes. OLake Go is fully open source under the Apache 2.0 license. You can explore the GitHub repository (already starred by 1K+ developers) and use it freely without hidden costs.

title: OLake Go product FAQ
text:
OLake Go product FAQ | olake.io product page

### Is there any enterprise plan?

We're actively working on providing enterprise support, from professional assistance and pilot programs to helping teams scale OLake Go in production. You can reach out at hello@olake.io to learn more.

title: OLake Go product FAQ
text:
OLake Go product FAQ | olake.io product page

### How can I contribute?

Join our Slack community, review the Contribution Guide, and explore "Good First Issues" on GitHub. Contributors can get their pull requests merged and be part of building the fastest open-source Iceberg-native ingestion tool.

title: OLake Go product FAQ
section_path: Why should I use OLake Go?
text:
OLake Go product FAQ | olake.io product page

### Why should I use OLake Go?

OLake Go makes data replication into Apache Iceberg seamless, faster, and cost-efficient. It handles real-time CDC, schema and partition evolution, full and incremental syncs, and compaction, all without vendor lock-in, so your Iceberg tables stay open, scalable, and ready for analytics.

title: OLake Go product FAQ
section_path: What data platforms and tools does OLake Go integrate with?
text:
OLake Go product FAQ | olake.io product page

### What data platforms and tools does OLake Go integrate with?

As of now, we integrate with Apache Iceberg and S3 as destinations. You can query it using popular query engines like Spark, AWS Athena, Snowflake, Databricks, and BigQuery.

title: OLake Fusion product FAQ
text:
OLake Fusion product FAQ | olake.io product page

### What is OLake Fusion?

OLake Fusion is a self-hosted open-source software that keeps your lakehouse tables efficient, compact, and query-ready as your data continuously grows. As Iceberg tables evolve through ingestion, updates, and deletes, they accumulate small files, delete files, and excess metadata, all of which degrade query performance and increase storage overhead over time. Fusion manages that for you automatically.

title: OLake Fusion product FAQ
section_path: When do I actually need table maintenance?
text:
OLake Fusion product FAQ | olake.io product page

### When do I actually need table maintenance?

Six situations call for it: frequent data ingestion or updates, accumulation of small files, presence of delete files, high partition cardinality, degrading query performance, and growing table size over time. If your tables are under continuous CDC pressure, you're in all six.

title: OLake Fusion product FAQ
section_path: Can I use OLake Fusion together with OLake Go?
text:
OLake Fusion product FAQ | olake.io product page

### Can I use OLake Fusion together with OLake Go?

Yes, that's the intended path. Iceberg Maintenance ships as a maintenance module inside the OLake UI from v0.4.0, so Go handles ingestion and Fusion handles maintenance from the same place. New users can start with a combined Ingestion + Maintenance setup, and existing OLake Go users just upgrade the UI (Docker or Helm/Kubernetes) to unlock the module, no separate tool to adopt. Our own compaction benchmark ran exactly this way: OLake Go ingesting the TPC-H lineitem table while Fusion compacted it.

title: OLake Fusion product FAQ
section_path: Can I use OLake Fusion on its own, without OLake Go?
text:
OLake Fusion product FAQ | olake.io product page

### Can I use OLake Fusion on its own, without OLake Go?

Yes, Fusion maintains Apache Iceberg tables through your Iceberg catalog, so it operates on the tables themselves rather than on OLake's ingestion pipeline.

title: OLake Fusion product FAQ
section_path: How much faster is Fusion than Apache Spark?
text:
OLake Fusion product FAQ | olake.io product page

### How much faster is Fusion than Apache Spark?

On a CDC-like TPC-H workload (300 GB, ~1.8 billion rows in lineitem), Fusion compacted in 27 minutes 2 seconds versus Spark rewrite_data_files at 55 minutes 47 seconds; 2.06× faster on identical infrastructure.

title: OLake Fusion product FAQ
section_path: Does it cost less than running Spark compaction?
text:
OLake Fusion product FAQ | olake.io product page

### Does it cost less than running Spark compaction?

Yes. On the same $2.36/hour infrastructure, the benchmark job cost $1.06 with Fusion and $2.19 with Spark, roughly half, because the job finishes in half the time.

title: OLake Fusion product FAQ
section_path: Do I have to pause ingestion or queries while compaction runs?
text:
OLake Fusion product FAQ | olake.io product page

### Do I have to pause ingestion or queries while compaction runs?

No. In the benchmark, compaction ran for two hours while CDC-style updates (~200,000 rows every 2 minutes) and repeated TPC-H Query 6 executions continued in parallel, specifically to measure how concurrent compaction affects query latency and stability.

title: OLake Fusion product FAQ
text:
OLake Fusion product FAQ | olake.io product page

### How often does compaction run?

Fusion uses tiered triggers rather than one blunt job: Lite every 20 minutes and Medium every 40 minutes in the benchmark, plus Full as a periodic deep-clean for much larger datasets, terabyte-scale tables where long-term small-file buildup is higher. At the benchmark's sub-100 GB destination size, Full wasn't needed.

title: OLake Fusion product FAQ
section_path: How do I deploy it, and what does it cost to license?
text:
OLake Fusion product FAQ | olake.io product page

### How do I deploy it, and what does it cost to license?

Fusion is open-source and is deployed on Docker or Kubernetes. You pay only for the compute and storage you provision.

title: OLake Fusion product FAQ
section_path: How much configuration does it need?
text:
OLake Fusion product FAQ | olake.io product page

### How much configuration does it need?

One parameter: target-size (512 MB in the benchmark). For comparison, the Spark rewrite_data_files job in the same test needed seven: strategy, target/max/min file size, concurrent rewrites, partial-progress, and delete-file threshold.

title: OLake Go destinations, Iceberg catalogs and their minimum versions
section_path: OLake Go destinations and Iceberg catalogs
text:
OLake Go destinations, Iceberg catalogs and their minimum versions | OLake fact card

# OLake Go destinations and Iceberg catalogs

OLake Go writes to two kinds of destination:

- Apache Iceberg tables, registered in an Iceberg catalog, with data and metadata files on object storage.
- Parquet files on object storage (Amazon S3, MinIO, Google Cloud Storage) or on a local path.

title: OLake Go destinations, Iceberg catalogs and their minimum versions
section_path: OLake Go destinations and Iceberg catalogs
text:
OLake Go destinations, Iceberg catalogs and their minimum versions | OLake fact card > OLake Go destinations and Iceberg catalogs

## Supported Iceberg catalogs

The catalog compatibility page lists 11 Iceberg catalogs. The minimum OLake Go version is the one the setup page states; "not stated" means the docs give none.

| Catalog | Setup guide | Minimum OLake Go version |
|---|---|---|
| AWS Glue | Glue catalog page | not stated |
| REST (Generic) | REST catalog page | not stated |
| REST Lakekeeper | REST catalog page | not stated |
| REST Nessie | REST catalog page | not stated |
| REST Apache Polaris | REST catalog page | not stated |
| REST Unity (Databricks Unity Catalog) | REST catalog page | not stated |
| S3 Tables | REST catalog page | not stated |
| REST BigLake (Google) | REST catalog page | 0.9.1 and above |
| REST Horizon (Snowflake Horizon Catalog) | REST catalog page | 0.11.0 and above |
| JDBC | JDBC catalog page | not stated |
| Hive Metastore | Hive catalog page | not stated |

- A custom catalog name is supported from v0.3.5; it may contain only lowercase letters and underscores (no spaces or special characters).

title: OLake Go destinations, Iceberg catalogs and their minimum versions
section_path: OLake Go destinations and Iceberg catalogs
text:
OLake Go destinations, Iceberg catalogs and their minimum versions | OLake fact card > OLake Go destinations and Iceberg catalogs

## Storage behind each catalog

- AWS Glue: data and metadata files in Amazon S3, metadata managed by the Glue Data Catalog; the S3 bucket should be in the same AWS region as the Glue catalog.
- Hive Metastore: object storage such as S3, GCS, MinIO or another S3-compatible system.
- JDBC catalog: a relational database such as PostgreSQL or MySQL holds the Iceberg metadata; data goes to S3, MinIO or another S3-compatible store.
- Azure: Iceberg on Azure Data Lake Storage (ADLS) Gen2 is documented with the Lakekeeper REST catalog.
- Google Cloud Storage: Iceberg on GCS is documented with the Hive catalog.

title: OLake Go destinations, Iceberg catalogs and their minimum versions
section_path: OLake Go destinations and Iceberg catalogs
text:
OLake Go destinations, Iceberg catalogs and their minimum versions | OLake fact card > OLake Go destinations and Iceberg catalogs

## When each catalog arrived (release notes)

- Hive catalog support: the 28-04-2025 release (which also renamed `catalog.json` to `streams.json`).
- Databricks Unity Catalog support: the v0.1.2 to v0.1.5 releases (June 26 to July 1, 2025).
- Custom catalog name: v0.3.5.
- Google BigLake catalog support (and BigLake multi-bucket catalogs): listed in the v0.9.0 release notes, while the REST catalog page says BigLake needs v0.9.1 and above.
- Snowflake Horizon Catalog support: v0.11.0.

title: OLake Go destinations, Iceberg catalogs and their minimum versions
section_path: OLake Go destinations and Iceberg catalogs
text:
OLake Go destinations, Iceberg catalogs and their minimum versions | OLake fact card > OLake Go destinations and Iceberg catalogs

## Parquet destination

- S3 Parquet writes Parquet files directly to an S3 bucket (AWS S3 or MinIO); Google Cloud Storage works through its S3-compatible API with HMAC keys used as the access key and secret key.
- The local Parquet writer writes to a local path (`local_path`, for example `/mnt/config` with Docker).

title: OLake features and the minimum component versions they need
text:
OLake features and the minimum component versions they need | OLake fact card

# Feature to minimum component versions

OLake has several separately versioned components: the OLake Go connectors (also called the OLake version or driver version), the OLake UI, the OLake worker and the Helm chart. Some features need minimum versions of several of them at once; upgrading only one component can make sync jobs fail.

title: OLake features and the minimum component versions they need
section_path: Delete formats (Upsert types) and the index DB
text:
OLake features and the minimum component versions they need | OLake fact card > Feature to minimum component versions

## Delete formats (Upsert types) and the index DB

- Choosing the Iceberg delete format (equality deletes, positional deletes or deletion vectors) needs OLake 0.11.0+, OLake UI 0.6.0+, Helm chart 0.0.28+ and OLake worker 0.3.11+.
- Positional deletes and deletion vectors need a persistent index store (a local Pebble DB, configured with `OLAKE_INDEX_DB_DIR`, `OLAKE_INDEX_DB_CACHE_SIZE` and `OLAKE_INDEX_DB_MAX_OPEN_FILES` on the temporal-worker); equality deletes, the default, need no index DB.
- Deletion vectors are Iceberg v3; equality and positional deletes are Iceberg v2. Switching between deletion vectors and equality or positional deletes on an existing job triggers Clear Destination.

title: OLake features and the minimum component versions they need
text:
OLake features and the minimum component versions they need | OLake fact card > Feature to minimum component versions

## Kafka

- Kafka as a source: OLake Go v0.3.0 and above.
- Kafka Upsert ingestion mode: OLake Go 0.12.1 and above with OLake UI 0.7.1 and above.

title: OLake features and the minimum component versions they need
text:
OLake features and the minimum component versions they need | OLake fact card > Feature to minimum component versions

## Log storage on S3

- Storing job logs on S3 instead of NFS needs OLake 0.12.0+, OLake UI 0.7.0+, OLake worker 0.4.0+ and, on Kubernetes, Helm chart 0.0.30+.
- On Kubernetes, NFS is still the default log storage mode but is deprecated, to be removed at the end of 2026, when S3 becomes the default.

title: OLake features and the minimum component versions they need
text:
OLake features and the minimum component versions they need | OLake fact card > Feature to minimum component versions

## OLake Fusion (Iceberg maintenance)

- The Maintenance module (OLake Fusion inside the OLake UI) is available from OLake UI v0.4.0.
- For conflict-free compaction of OLake-ingested tables, the OLake Go (ingestion) driver must be v0.7.0 or higher.

title: OLake features and the minimum component versions they need
text:
OLake features and the minimum component versions they need | OLake fact card > Feature to minimum component versions

## UI, alerts and monitoring

- Alerts and notifications: OLake UI 0.2.3+ and worker 0.2.3+.
- Target Query Engine (a job setting): OLake UI 0.6.0 and above.
- Clear Destination: stable from OLake Go v0.3.0.
- The `/metrics` endpoint: OLake UI 0.5.0 or higher; the `olake_sync_bytes_read`, `olake_process_cpu_usage_ratio` and `olake_process_memory_usage_bytes` metrics need OLake Go v0.9.0 or later.

title: OLake features and the minimum component versions they need
text:
OLake features and the minimum component versions they need | OLake fact card > Feature to minimum component versions

## Streams, filters and columns

- Data filter during CDC and Incremental syncs: OLake Go connector v0.6.0 and OLake UI v0.4.1; it only works for jobs created on connector v0.6.0 or later.
- Column selection and automatic sync of new columns: OLake Go v0.4.0 and OLake UI v0.3.1.
- Source Naming Convention: OLake Go v0.7.7 and OLake UI v0.4.7.
- Driver-specific CDC metadata columns (for example `_cdc_lsn` for Postgres, `_cdc_binlog_file_name` and `_cdc_binlog_file_pos` for MySQL, `_cdc_start_lsn` and `_cdc_seqval` for MSSQL): the docs say the feature is available starting from v0.3.16.
- MySQL `INT UNSIGNED` maps to `bigint` from OLake Go 0.4.1 (to `int` before).

title: OLake features and the minimum component versions they need
text:
OLake features and the minimum component versions they need | OLake fact card > Feature to minimum component versions

## Catalogs and Helm

- Google BigLake catalog: OLake Go 0.9.1 and above. Snowflake Horizon catalog: OLake Go 0.11.0 and above. Custom catalog names: v0.3.5 and above.
- From Helm chart 0.0.11, the chart disables Elasticsearch by default and uses PostgreSQL for both metadata and Temporal visibility.

title: Known contradictions between OLake pages
text:
Known contradictions between OLake pages | OLake fact card

# Known contradictions between OLake pages

Places where two first-party OLake pages disagree. When answering, cite both pages and say they differ.

title: Known contradictions between OLake pages
text:
Known contradictions between OLake pages | OLake fact card

## OLake Fusion default compaction schedule

- The "Configure your first compaction" page says default schedules are applied automatically: Lite every 1 hour, Medium every 8 hours, Full never (not scheduled).
- The compaction configuration page says that if a configuration is left unset (for example in Bulk Configure), the defaults are 24 hours for each compaction type and a 512 MB target file size.
- The OLake Fusion product FAQ quotes Lite every 20 minutes and Medium every 40 minutes, but as the cadence used in a benchmark, not as defaults.
- Both docs pages give 512 MB as the default target file size (the FAQ's benchmark also used 512 MB).

title: Known contradictions between OLake pages
text:
Known contradictions between OLake pages | OLake fact card

## MySQL `binlog_row_metadata=FULL`

- The MySQL connector page lists `binlog_row_metadata=FULL` under the required binary logging settings for CDC.
- The v0.10.0 release notes say MySQL CDC works without `binlog_row_metadata=FULL`, for MySQL and MariaDB setups where full row metadata is unavailable.

title: Known contradictions between OLake pages
text:
Known contradictions between OLake pages | OLake fact card

## MySQL `initial_wait_time` examples

- On the MySQL connector page, the example `source.json` and the field table use `"initial_wait_time": 10`, while the `update_method` row of the same table shows `{"initial_wait_time": 120}`; the local setup page's example uses 1.
- `initial_wait_time` is the maximum time in seconds to wait before the binlog syncer is considered idle; the troubleshooting section says to raise it when locating the saved binlog position takes longer than the configured value.

title: Known contradictions between OLake pages
text:
Known contradictions between OLake pages | OLake fact card

## Google BigLake catalog version

title: OLake Go sources and the sync modes each one supports
section_path: OLake Go sources and their sync modes
text:
OLake Go sources and the sync modes each one supports | OLake fact card

# OLake Go sources and their sync modes

The sources OLake Go (the ingestion product) can read from, with the sync modes each one supports. Every source supports Full Refresh + Incremental except Kafka.

| Source | Full Refresh | Full Refresh + Incremental | Full Refresh + CDC | CDC Only (Strict CDC) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PostgreSQL | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| MySQL (the MySQL connector also covers MariaDB) | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| MongoDB | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| MSSQL (SQL Server) | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| Oracle Database | yes | yes | no | no |
| IBM DB2 | yes | yes | no | no |
| Apache Kafka | no | no | no | yes (its only mode) |
| Amazon S3 and S3-compatible storage | yes | yes | no | no |

- No CDC for Oracle, DB2 or S3: neither Full Refresh + CDC nor CDC Only is supported for them; use Full Refresh or Full Refresh + Incremental.
- Kafka supports only one sync mode: CDC Only. Full Refresh and Incremental are not available for Kafka.

title: OLake Go sources and the sync modes each one supports
section_path: OLake Go sources and their sync modes
text:
OLake Go sources and the sync modes each one supports | OLake fact card > OLake Go sources and their sync modes

## Sync mode names

- Full Refresh: copies the whole table every run (`full_refresh` in streams.json); it keeps no state file.
- Full Refresh + Incremental: a full refresh first, then only rows whose cursor field is greater than the last synced value (`incremental`). An auto-increment cursor picks up new rows only; an `updated_at`-style cursor also picks up updates; deletes are never tracked.
- Full Refresh + CDC: a full refresh first, then inserts, updates and deletes from the change stream (`cdc`).
- CDC Only, also called Strict CDC (`strict_cdc`): skips the full refresh and processes only changes after CDC begins.
- Changing a stream's sync mode triggers Clear Destination.

title: OLake Go sources and the sync modes each one supports
section_path: OLake Go sources and their sync modes
text:
OLake Go sources and the sync modes each one supports | OLake fact card > OLake Go sources and their sync modes

## PostgreSQL

- Sync modes: Full Refresh, Full Refresh + Incremental, Full Refresh + CDC and CDC Only.
- Requires PostgreSQL 10 or above. CDC uses the native `pgoutput` plugin; the `wal2json`-based CDC method is deprecated.

title: OLake Go sources and the sync modes each one supports
section_path: OLake Go sources and their sync modes
text:
OLake Go sources and the sync modes each one supports | OLake fact card > OLake Go sources and their sync modes

## MySQL and MariaDB

- Sync modes: Full Refresh, Full Refresh + Incremental, Full Refresh + CDC and CDC Only.
- The MySQL connector also supports MariaDB as a CDC source.
- Requires MySQL 5.7+. CDC reads the binary log: the MySQL page lists `log_bin=ON`, `binlog_format=ROW`, `binlog_row_image=FULL` and `binlog_row_metadata=FULL` as required, a unique `server-id`, and the REPLICATION SLAVE, REPLICATION CLIENT and SELECT privileges.
- The v0.10.0 release notes add MySQL CDC without `binlog_row_metadata=FULL`, for MySQL and MariaDB setups where full row metadata is unavailable, so the two pages disagree on whether that setting is required.

title: OLake Go sources and the sync modes each one supports
section_path: OLake Go sources and their sync modes
text:
OLake Go sources and the sync modes each one supports | OLake fact card > OLake Go sources and their sync modes

## MongoDB

- Sync modes: Full Refresh, Full Refresh + Incremental, Full Refresh + CDC and CDC Only.
- Requires MongoDB 4.0 or higher. CDC requires replica set mode (`--replSet`) with the oplog; without it, use Incremental sync.
- CDC is not a continuous always-on process: each CDC sync runs through the orchestrator (a job run).

title: OLake Go sources and the sync modes each one supports
section_path: OLake Go sources and their sync modes
text:
OLake Go sources and the sync modes each one supports | OLake fact card > OLake Go sources and their sync modes

## MSSQL (SQL Server)

- Sync modes: Full Refresh, Full Refresh + Incremental, Full Refresh + CDC and CDC Only.
- Requires SQL Server 2017 or higher. CDC must be enabled on the database and on each table to capture; CDC change tables keep events for 3 days by default, and expired events require a full backfill.

title: OLake Go sources and the sync modes each one supports
section_path: OLake Go sources and their sync modes
text:
OLake Go sources and the sync modes each one supports | OLake fact card > OLake Go sources and their sync modes

## Oracle

- Sync modes: Full Refresh and Full Refresh + Incremental only. Oracle has no CDC support in OLake Go: neither Full Refresh + CDC nor CDC Only is available.
- Requires Oracle Database 11g or above (tested with 19c and 23ai); the user needs CREATE SESSION and SELECT on the tables.

title: OLake Go sources and the sync modes each one supports
section_path: OLake Go sources and their sync modes
text:
OLake Go sources and the sync modes each one supports | OLake fact card > OLake Go sources and their sync modes

## IBM DB2

- Sync modes: Full Refresh and Full Refresh + Incremental only; no CDC.
- Requires DB2 11.5.3 or higher. The IBM Data Server ODBC and CLI driver is not supported on Linux arm64; AMD64 is the recommended CPU architecture.

title: OLake Go sources and the sync modes each one supports
section_path: OLake Go sources and their sync modes
text:
OLake Go sources and the sync modes each one supports | OLake fact card > OLake Go sources and their sync modes

## Apache Kafka

- Sync mode: CDC Only, the only mode the Kafka connector supports (no Full Refresh, no Incremental).
- Requires Kafka 2.4.0 or higher; Kafka as a source is available from OLake Go v0.3.0; tested with Amazon MSK.
- Messages must be JSON or Avro (Avro needs a Confluent Schema Registry). Messages already past the topic's retention period cannot be synced.
- Ingestion mode defaults to Append for Kafka. Upsert needs a deduplication key, uses positional deletes only, and requires OLake Go 0.12.1+ and OLake UI 0.7.1+.

title: OLake Go sources and the sync modes each one supports
section_path: OLake Go sources and their sync modes
text:
OLake Go sources and the sync modes each one supports | OLake fact card > OLake Go sources and their sync modes

## Amazon S3

- Sync modes: Full Refresh and Full Refresh + Incremental only; no CDC.
- Incremental sync uses each file's S3 `LastModified` timestamp as the cursor (`_last_modified_time`); a file that is modified and re-uploaded is synced again.
- Formats: CSV, JSON (JSONL and array), XML and Parquet, with transparent gzip decompression; works with AWS S3 and S3-compatible services (MinIO, LocalStack).

title: What OLake does not support, or the docs do not document
text:
What OLake does not support, or the docs do not document | OLake fact card

# Unsupported or undocumented in OLake

Things people ask about that OLake does not support, or that its docs do not document, with the page that lists what is supported.

title: What OLake does not support, or the docs do not document
text:
What OLake does not support, or the docs do not document | OLake fact card > Unsupported or undocumented in OLake

## Sources that are not supported

- OLake Go reads from eight sources: PostgreSQL, MySQL (and MariaDB), MongoDB, MSSQL (SQL Server), Oracle Database, IBM DB2, Apache Kafka and Amazon S3.
- Any other system is not a supported source, for example Snowflake, Google BigQuery, Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon Redshift, Cassandra or Elasticsearch.
- Snowflake, BigQuery and Redshift appear in the docs as query engines that read the Iceberg tables OLake writes (and Snowflake Horizon and Google BigLake as Iceberg catalogs), not as sources.

title: What OLake does not support, or the docs do not document
section_path: Sync modes that are not supported
text:
What OLake does not support, or the docs do not document | OLake fact card > Unsupported or undocumented in OLake

## Sync modes that are not supported

- CDC (Full Refresh + CDC or CDC Only) is not supported for Oracle, DB2 or S3; they support Full Refresh and Full Refresh + Incremental.
- Kafka supports only CDC Only: no Full Refresh and no Incremental.
- DB2: the IBM Data Server ODBC and CLI driver is not supported on Linux arm64; AMD64 is recommended.

title: What OLake does not support, or the docs do not document
text:
What OLake does not support, or the docs do not document | OLake fact card > Unsupported or undocumented in OLake

## Destinations that are not supported

- OLake Go writes only Apache Iceberg tables and Parquet files. Other table formats and warehouses (for example Delta Lake, Apache Hudi, or loading straight into Snowflake, BigQuery or ClickHouse tables) are not OLake destinations; query engines read the Iceberg tables OLake writes instead.

title: What OLake does not support, or the docs do not document
text:
What OLake does not support, or the docs do not document | OLake fact card > Unsupported or undocumented in OLake

## Not available yet

- Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) columns, which would store values with unsupported type changes instead of failing the sync, are marked "Coming soon" on the docs home page.

title: What OLake does not support, or the docs do not document
text:
What OLake does not support, or the docs do not document | OLake fact card > Unsupported or undocumented in OLake

## OLake Fusion (table maintenance) scope

- OLake Fusion's documented maintenance is compaction (Lite, Medium and Full) plus table observability (file metrics and a health score).
- Snapshot expiry: the Fusion v0.1.0 to v0.1.4 release notes say automatic snapshot expiry was disabled, to keep snapshots from being removed automatically.
- Orphan-file cleanup: not documented for OLake Fusion.

title: What OLake does not support, or the docs do not document
text:
What OLake does not support, or the docs do not document | OLake fact card > Unsupported or undocumented in OLake

## Login, security and commercial terms

- Single sign-on (SSO, SAML, LDAP or OIDC login) for the OLake UI is not documented.
- On Kubernetes, OLake does not support setting a `securityContext` for the `nfsServer`.
- Pricing, SLAs and enterprise plans are not published. The OLake Go FAQ says enterprise support is in the works and points to hello@olake.io, and that OLake Go is open source under the Apache 2.0 license. The OLake Fusion FAQ says Fusion is open source and you pay only for the compute and storage you provision.

    OLake Go

  OLake Go is a high-performance, open-source data ingestion engine for replicating databases, S3, and Kafka into
  Apache Iceberg (or plain Parquet).

  Built for scalable, real-time pipelines, OLake Go provides a simple web UI and CLI - used to ingest into vendor-lock-in free Iceberg tables supporting all the query-engines/warehouses.

  Read the docs and benchmarks at
  olake.io/docs.
  Join our active community on
  Slack.

> [!NOTE]
> 🎉 **OLake Fusion is now live!** — Automate your Apache Iceberg Table Maintenance. Check it out here → [github.com/datazip-inc/olake-fusion](https://github.com/datazip-inc/olake-fusion) 🎉

## OLake Go — Super-fast Sync to Apache Iceberg

**OLake Go** supports replication from **transactional databases** such as **PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, Oracle, DB2, and MSSQL**, **event-streaming systems like Apache Kafka** and **Object-store like S3**, into open data lakehouse formats such as **Apache Iceberg** or **Plain Parquet** — delivering blazing-fast performance with minimal infrastructure cost.

#### Creating Your First Job

With the UI running, you can create a data pipeline in a few steps:

1. **Configure Source:** Navigate to **Source** tab and click **Create Source**. Set up your source connection.
2. **Configure Destination:** Navigate to **Destination** tab and click **Create Destination**. Set up your destination.
3. **Create a Job:** Navigate to the **Jobs** tab and click **Create Job**. 
4. **Configure & Run:** Give your job a name, set a schedule, select your source and destination and click **Next** to finish.
5. **Select Streams:** Choose which tables to sync and configure their sync mode (`CDC`, `Full Refresh` or `Incremental`).

### 🛠️ CLI Usage (Advanced)

For advanced users and automation, OLake Go's core logic is exposed via a powerful CLI. The core framework handles state management, configuration validation, logging, and type detection. It interacts with drivers using four main commands:

* `spec`: Returns a render-able JSON Schema for a connector's configuration.
* `check`: Validates connection configurations for sources and destinations.
* `discover`: Returns all available streams (e.g., tables) and their schemas from a source.
* `sync`: Executes the data replication job, extracting from the source and writing to the destination.
* `clear-destination` : Clears data in the destination, only for the selected streams defined in `streams.json`.

**Find out more about CLI [here](https://olake.io/docs/install/docker-cli/).**

text:
olake: destination/iceberg/README.md | GitHub repo datazip-inc/olake

# Iceberg-writer

Writes to apache-iceberg. This writer takes configuration of catalog and s3 buckets and writes data received from the Olake source.

## How It Works

Iceberg writer writes data primarily as a equality delete which doesn't requires spark. 

For backfill --> Works in append mode

For CDC --> Works in Upsert mode by creating delete files

### Current Architecture :

> Golang Code  --gRPC-->  Java (This Project)  --Write to Iceberg-->  S3 + Iceberg Catalog

Important reason why we are using Java to write is, current Golang-iceberg project doesn't support Equality delete writes. We plan to move this to iceberg-rust to improve on memory footprint.

1. Flow starts with iceberg.go file. 
2. We create Java rpc server by a process call.
3. Send records via rpc in batches of 256 mb (in-memory object size, not a real parquet size)

### Java Iceberg Writer/sink :

Its based in the directory olake-iceberg-java-writer. Read more ./olake-iceberg-java-writer/README.md on how to run it in standalone mode and test.

## Environment Variables

### OLAKE_DEBUG_MODE

Set this environment variable to enable debug mode for the Java Iceberg writer. When enabled, the Java process will start with remote debugging options, allowing you to attach a debugger on port 5005.

**Note:** Debug mode is only enabled during sync operations (not during check operations) to avoid blocking the connection check process.

```bash
# Enable debug mode
export OLAKE_DEBUG_MODE=1

# Run your sync command
olake sync --config source.json --destination destination.json --catalog catalog.json
```

## How to run

### Local Minio + JDBC Catalog (Local test setup):

Make sure you have docker installed before you run this

```shell
cd destination/iceberg/local-test
docker compose up
```

This will create 
1. postgres --> JDBC catalog
2. Minio --> For AWS S3 like filesystem setup on your local
3. Spark --> Querying Iceberg data.

Now create a writer.json for iceberg writer as follows : 

```json
{
  "type": "ICEBERG",
  "writer": {
    "catalog_type": "jdbc",
    "jdbc_url": "jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/iceberg",
    "jdbc_username": "iceberg",
    "jdbc_password": "<redacted>",
    "iceberg_s3_path": "s3a://warehouse",
    "s3_endpoint": "http://localhost:9000",
    "s3_use_ssl": false,
    "s3_path_style": true,
    "aws_access_key": "admin",
    "aws_secret_key": "<redacted>"
  }
}  
```

And run the sync normally as mentioned in the getting started doc.
